Humains — Hildor

Les Humains, appelés Hildor par les Elfes, sont les Seconds-Nés des Enfants d’Ilúvatar. Ils s’éveillèrent dans l’Est de la Terre du Milieu, dans une région appelée Hildórien, au cours du Premier Âge. Les Elfes les nommèrent Hildor, « les Suivants », parce qu’ils apparurent après les Premiers-Nés. Les termes quenya Atani et sindarin Edain, « Second Peuple », furent également employés pour les désigner.

Les Hommes diffèrent des Elfes avant tout par le Don des Hommes : ils sont mortels. Leur vie est brève à l’échelle des Elfes et des Nains, mais ils se renouvellent rapidement, fondent de nouvelles communautés et s’adaptent à des environnements très différents. Ils sont nombreux, variés et plus vulnérables que les Elfes aux maladies et aux températures extrêmes, mais ils se lassent rarement de la vie.

Origines et diversité

Les premiers siècles de l’histoire humaine sont mal connus dans l’Ouest. Les Hommes se dispersèrent très tôt et leurs peuples développèrent des langues, des coutumes et des modes de vie distincts. Lorsque certains atteignirent le Beleriand, plusieurs lignées existaient déjà.

Cette diversité est un caractère essentiel des Hildor. La Race représente donc la nature humaine commune, tandis que les Cultures déterminent l’éducation, la langue, les compétences, les croyances et les usages d’un personnage. Un Rohirrim, un Beffraen, un Dorwinrim, un Haruze, un Variag ou un Homme des Bois sont tous des Humains, même si leurs sociétés et leurs aptitudes culturelles diffèrent fortement.

Le Don des Hommes

Les Hommes sont mortels et leur destin après la mort est différent de celui des Elfes. Dans la tradition des Sages, cette mortalité est un don d’Ilúvatar et non une imperfection. Les esprits des Hommes quittent les limites du monde selon une destinée que les Valar eux-mêmes ne connaissent pas pleinement.

La conscience de cette mortalité influence fortement les sociétés humaines. Elle peut favoriser l’ambition, le désir de descendance, la volonté de laisser une œuvre durable ou la recherche de gloire. Elle peut aussi engendrer la peur de la mort et le désir de prolonger artificiellement la vie. Sauron exploita souvent cette faiblesse, notamment chez les Númenóréens.

Grands groupes humains

Les traditions occidentales distinguent les Hauts Hommes, les Hommes communs et parfois les Hommes du Nord. Les Hauts Hommes descendent des Edain alliés aux Elfes contre Morgoth et sont à l’origine des Númenóréens puis des Dúnedain. Dans merp-ui, les Dúnedain sont traités comme une Race distincte afin de représenter leur longévité, leur stature et leur héritage particuliers.

Les Hommes communs représentent la majorité des peuples humains. Leur apparence et leurs cultures sont extrêmement diverses. Les Hommes du Nord sont proches de certaines lignées des Edain, mais n’ont pas bénéficié du même contact prolongé avec les Eldar ni des dons accordés aux habitants de Númenor.

Apparence

Les Humains présentent la plus grande diversité physique parmi les principales Races jouables. Leur taille, leur corpulence, la couleur de leur peau, de leurs cheveux et de leurs yeux varient selon les peuples et les régions. Les Hommes communs sont en moyenne plus petits et plus trapus que les Dúnedain, mais aucune apparence unique ne peut être considérée comme typiquement humaine.

Les cheveux peuvent être noirs, bruns, châtains, roux ou blonds. Les yeux peuvent être noirs, bruns, gris, bleus, verts ou noisette. La pilosité faciale est courante chez de nombreuses populations masculines. Les différences physiques doivent être déterminées par la Culture et l’origine régionale plutôt que par un modèle racial unique.

Longévité, maturité et santé

La plupart des Hommes vivent entre cinquante et quatre-vingts ans, bien que l’espérance de vie varie fortement selon les conditions de vie et les lignées. Certains individus dépassent quatre-vingt-dix ans. Les Hommes atteignent leur maturité beaucoup plus rapidement que les Elfes et les Nains, ce qui leur permet de renouveler rapidement leurs générations.

Ils sont sensibles aux maladies, aux infections, aux poisons et aux températures extrêmes. Cette vulnérabilité les a conduits à développer de nombreuses traditions de médecine, d’herboristerie et de soins. Les résistances particulières au froid, à la chaleur, aux maladies ou aux privations doivent provenir d’une Culture, d’un Talent ou de l’équipement plutôt que de la Race elle-même.

Endurance, sommeil et sens

L’endurance humaine est moyenne mais très variable. Des soldats, cavaliers, marins, chasseurs ou voyageurs entraînés peuvent soutenir des efforts importants pendant de longues périodes. Leur capacité à supporter la fatigue dépend largement de l’entraînement et de la volonté.

Les Humains ont besoin d’un sommeil régulier et ne possèdent pas de vision nocturne particulière. Leur vision, leur ouïe et leurs autres sens se situent dans la moyenne. Une aptitude supérieure à la perception, au pistage ou à la survie doit donc être apportée par la Culture ou l’apprentissage.

Adaptabilité

La principale caractéristique des Humains est leur capacité à s’adapter rapidement. Ils vivent dans les plaines, les montagnes, les forêts, les déserts, les régions froides, les marais, les côtes et les grandes cités. En quelques générations, une communauté peut modifier son habitat, son alimentation, ses techniques de guerre, ses institutions et sa langue pour répondre à un nouvel environnement.

Cette faculté explique la grande variété des sociétés humaines. Les Hildor peuvent former des villages agricoles, des tribus nomades, des cités marchandes, des royaumes féodaux, des sociétés pastorales ou des empires centralisés.

Famille et société

Les Humains ont généralement davantage d’enfants que les Elfes ou les Nains. Les formes de famille, les règles de mariage, les successions et la place des clans varient considérablement d’une Culture à l’autre. La Race humaine n’impose donc pas de structure familiale particulière.

Il en va de même pour les formes de gouvernement. Les Hommes peuvent vivre sous l’autorité d’un chef de clan, d’un conseil, d’un roi, d’un prince, d’une cité autonome ou d’une administration complexe. Les institutions humaines évoluent rapidement à l’échelle de l’histoire de la Terre du Milieu.

Artisanat, techniques et guerre

Les Hommes peuvent atteindre un haut niveau d’artisanat, d’ingénierie et d’organisation. Ils pratiquent l’agriculture, la métallurgie, la construction, la navigation, l’élevage, le commerce et la fortification. Ils ne possèdent pas l’affinité particulière des Khazâd avec la pierre et le métal ni l’ancien savoir des Eldar, mais ils diffusent rapidement les techniques nouvelles.

Ils ont développé presque toutes les formes de guerre connues : infanterie, cavalerie, archers, lanciers, marins, éclaireurs et troupes lourdes. Les armes et armures favorites dépendent entièrement de la Culture et des ressources disponibles.

Langues, religion et magie

Il n’existe pas de langue humaine unique. Le westron devient la principale langue commune du nord-ouest de la Terre du Milieu aux Âges tardifs, mais l’adûnaïque, le rohirrique, le dunael, le haradaïque, le varadja, le logathig, le nahaiduk et de nombreux autres parlers restent liés à des peuples particuliers.

Les croyances humaines sont tout aussi diverses. Certains peuples reconnaissent clairement Eru et les Valar ; d’autres ont conservé des traditions anciennes ou développé des religions locales. Certaines sociétés ont également subi l’influence de Morgoth ou de Sauron. Les Humains peuvent pratiquer toutes les grandes formes de magie prévues par RMU lorsque leur Culture et leur formation le permettent.

Relations avec les autres peuples

Les rapports entre les Hommes et les Elfes vont de l’alliance étroite à la méfiance. Les relations avec les Khazâd sont souvent fondées sur le commerce, les métaux, les outils et les produits agricoles. Les Hobbits vivent généralement en paix avec les communautés humaines voisines.

Les Hommes occupent aussi une place centrale dans les guerres de l’Ombre. Certains furent parmi les plus grands adversaires de Morgoth et de Sauron, tandis que d’autres devinrent leurs serviteurs. Les Nazgûl eux-mêmes étaient autrefois des Hommes.

Professions et place dans la création de personnage

La Race Humains — Hildor n’interdit normalement aucune profession générale. Les restrictions doivent provenir de la Culture, de l’époque ou du contexte particulier du personnage. Cette Race est disponible durant les quatre Âges.

Après avoir choisi la Race Humains, le joueur sélectionne une Culture humaine appropriée à son époque et à son origine. Les Dúnedain sont traités séparément dans merp-ui en raison de leurs caractéristiques héritées de Númenor. Humans — Hildor

Humans, called Hildor by the Elves, are the Secondborn of the Children of Ilúvatar. They awoke in the East of Middle-earth, in a land called Hildórien, during the First Age. The Elves named them Hildor, “the Followers”, because they appeared after the Firstborn. The Quenya term Atani and the Sindarin Edain, “Second People”, were also used for them.

Humans differ from Elves above all through the Gift of Men: they are mortal. Their lives are brief by the measure of Elves and Dwarves, yet their generations renew quickly, they establish new communities, and they adapt to widely different environments. They are numerous and diverse, more vulnerable than Elves to disease and extremes of climate, but they rarely grow weary of life.

Origins and diversity

The first centuries of human history are poorly known in the West. Men dispersed early, and their peoples developed distinct languages, customs, and ways of life. By the time some reached Beleriand, several lineages already existed.

This diversity is essential to the Hildor. The Race therefore represents shared human nature, while Cultures determine a character’s upbringing, language, skills, beliefs, and customs. A Rohir, Beffraen, Dorwinrim, Haruze, Variag, or Woodman are all Humans even though their societies and cultural abilities differ greatly.

The Gift of Men

Men are mortal, and their fate after death differs from that of the Elves. In the tradition of the Wise, mortality is a gift of Ilúvatar rather than an imperfection. The spirits of Men leave the bounds of the world according to a destiny that even the Valar do not fully know.

Awareness of mortality strongly shapes human societies. It may foster ambition, the desire for descendants, the wish to leave an enduring work, or the pursuit of glory. It can also create fear of death and the desire to prolong life unnaturally. Sauron often exploited this weakness, most notably among the Númenóreans.

Major human groups

Western traditions distinguish High Men, Common Men, and sometimes Northmen. High Men descend from the Edain who allied with the Elves against Morgoth and became the ancestors of the Númenóreans and later the Dúnedain. In MERP-UI, the Dúnedain are treated as a separate Race to represent their particular longevity, stature, and heritage.

Common Men make up most human peoples. Their appearances and cultures are extraordinarily varied. Northmen are close to some lineages of the Edain, but they did not benefit from the same prolonged contact with the Eldar or from the gifts granted to the people of Númenor.

Appearance

Humans show the greatest physical diversity among the principal playable Races. Height, build, skin tone, hair, and eye colour vary by people and region. Common Men are on average shorter and stockier than the Dúnedain, but no single appearance can be considered typically human.

Hair may be black, brown, chestnut, red, or blond. Eyes may be black, brown, grey, blue, green, or hazel. Facial hair is common among many male populations. Physical differences should be determined by Culture and regional origin rather than by a single racial model.

Longevity, maturity, and health

Most Men live between fifty and eighty years, although life expectancy varies greatly with living conditions and lineage. Some individuals live beyond ninety. Humans reach maturity much faster than Elves and Dwarves, allowing their generations to renew quickly.

They are susceptible to disease, infection, poison, and extremes of temperature. This vulnerability has led to many traditions of medicine, herbalism, and healing. Particular resistance to cold, heat, disease, or deprivation should come from Culture, a Talent, or equipment rather than from the Race itself.

Endurance, sleep, and senses

Human endurance is average but highly variable. Trained soldiers, riders, sailors, hunters, and travellers can sustain considerable effort for long periods. Their ability to withstand fatigue depends largely on training and willpower.

Humans require regular sleep and possess no special night vision. Their sight, hearing, and other senses are broadly average. Superior ability in perception, tracking, or survival should therefore come from Culture or training.

Adaptability

The defining strength of Humans is their ability to adapt quickly. They live on plains, in mountains and forests, deserts and cold lands, marshes, coasts, and great cities. Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

This ability explains the great variety of human societies. The Hildor may form farming villages, nomadic tribes, trading cities, feudal kingdoms, pastoral societies, or centralized empires.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Crafts, technology, and war

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

Languages, religion, and magic

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Professions and character creation

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.

Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

Languages, religion, and magic

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Professions and character creation

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.

Humans — Hildor

Humans, called Hildor by the Elves, are the Secondborn of the Children of Ilúvatar. They awoke in the East of Middle-earth, in a land called Hildórien, during the First Age. The Elves named them Hildor, “the Followers”, because they appeared after the Firstborn. The Quenya term Atani and the Sindarin Edain, “Second People”, were also used for them.

Humans differ from Elves above all through the Gift of Men: they are mortal. Their lives are brief by the measure of Elves and Dwarves, yet their generations renew quickly, they establish new communities, and they adapt to widely different environments. Origins and diversity

This diversity is essential to the Hildor. The Race therefore represents shared human nature, while Cultures determine a character’s upbringing, language, skills, beliefs, and customs. The Gift of Men

It can also create fear of death and the desire to prolong life unnaturally. Sauron often exploited this weakness, most notably among the Númenóreans.

Major human groups

Western traditions distinguish High Men, Common Men, and sometimes Northmen. High Men descend from the Edain who allied with the Elves against Morgoth and became the ancestors of the Númenóreans and later the Dúnedain. Longevity, maturity, and health

Most Men live between fifty and eighty years, although life expectancy varies greatly with living conditions and lineage. Some individuals live beyond ninety. Humans reach maturity much faster than Elves and Dwarves, allowing their generations to renew quickly.

They are susceptible to disease, infection, poison, and extremes of temperature. This vulnerability has led to many traditions of medicine, herbalism, and healing. Endurance, sleep, and senses

Human endurance is average but highly variable. Trained soldiers, riders, sailors, hunters, and travellers can sustain considerable effort for long periods. Their ability to withstand fatigue depends largely on training and willpower.

Humans require regular sleep and possess no special night vision. Their sight, hearing, and other senses are broadly average. Superior ability in perception, tracking, or survival should therefore come from Culture or training.

Adaptability

The defining strength of Humans is their ability to adapt quickly. They live on plains, in mountains and forests, deserts and cold lands, marshes, coasts, and great cities. Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

This ability explains the great variety of human societies. The Hildor may form farming villages, nomadic tribes, trading cities, feudal kingdoms, pastoral societies, or centralized empires.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Crafts, technology, and war

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

Languages, religion, and magic

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Professions and character creation

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.

The first centuries of human history are poorly known in the West. Men dispersed early, and their peoples developed distinct languages, customs, and ways of life. By the time some reached Beleriand, several lineages already existed.

This diversity is essential to the Hildor. The Race therefore represents shared human nature, while Cultures determine a character’s upbringing, language, skills, beliefs, and customs. A Rohir, Beffraen, Dorwinrim, Haruze, Variag, or Woodman are all Humans even though their societies and cultural abilities differ greatly.

The Gift of Men

Men are mortal, and their fate after death differs from that of the Elves. In the tradition of the Wise, mortality is a gift of Ilúvatar rather than an imperfection. The spirits of Men leave the bounds of the world according to a destiny that even the Valar do not fully know.

Awareness of mortality strongly shapes human societies. It may foster ambition, the desire for descendants, the wish to leave an enduring work, or the pursuit of glory. It can also create fear of death and the desire to prolong life unnaturally. Sauron often exploited this weakness, most notably among the Númenóreans.

Major human groups

Western traditions distinguish High Men, Common Men, and sometimes Northmen. High Men descend from the Edain who allied with the Elves against Morgoth and became the ancestors of the Númenóreans and later the Dúnedain. In MERP-UI, the Dúnedain are treated as a separate Race to represent their particular longevity, stature, and heritage.

Common Men make up most human peoples. Their appearances and cultures are extraordinarily varied. Northmen are close to some lineages of the Edain, but they did not benefit from the same prolonged contact with the Eldar or from the gifts granted to the people of Númenor.

Appearance

Humans show the greatest physical diversity among the principal playable Races. Height, build, skin tone, hair, and eye colour vary by people and region. Common Men are on average shorter and stockier than the Dúnedain, but no single appearance can be considered typically human.

Hair may be black, brown, chestnut, red, or blond. Eyes may be black, brown, grey, blue, green, or hazel. Facial hair is common among many male populations. Physical differences should be determined by Culture and regional origin rather than by a single racial model.

Longevity, maturity, and health

Most Men live between fifty and eighty years, although life expectancy varies greatly with living conditions and lineage. Some individuals live beyond ninety. Humans reach maturity much faster than Elves and Dwarves, allowing their generations to renew quickly.

They are susceptible to disease, infection, poison, and extremes of temperature. This vulnerability has led to many traditions of medicine, herbalism, and healing. Particular resistance to cold, heat, disease, or deprivation should come from Culture, a Talent, or equipment rather than from the Race itself.

Endurance, sleep, and senses

Human endurance is average but highly variable. Trained soldiers, riders, sailors, hunters, and travellers can sustain considerable effort for long periods. Their ability to withstand fatigue depends largely on training and willpower.

Humans require regular sleep and possess no special night vision. Their sight, hearing, and other senses are broadly average. Superior ability in perception, tracking, or survival should therefore come from Culture or training.

Adaptability

The defining strength of Humans is their ability to adapt quickly. They live on plains, in mountains and forests, deserts and cold lands, marshes, coasts, and great cities. Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

This ability explains the great variety of human societies. The Hildor may form farming villages, nomadic tribes, trading cities, feudal kingdoms, pastoral societies, or centralized empires.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Crafts, technology, and war

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

Languages, religion, and magic

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Humans — Hildor

Humans, called Hildor by the Elves, are the Secondborn of the Children of Ilúvatar. They awoke in the East of Middle-earth, in a land called Hildórien, during the First Age. It can also create fear of death and the desire to prolong life unnaturally. Sauron often exploited this weakness, most notably among the Númenóreans.

Hair may be black, brown, chestnut, red, or blond. Eyes may be black, brown, grey, blue, green, or hazel. Facial hair is common among many male populations. Physical differences should be determined by Culture and regional origin rather than by a single racial model.

Most Men live between fifty and eighty years, although life expectancy varies greatly with living conditions and lineage. Some individuals live beyond ninety. Humans reach maturity much faster than Elves and Dwarves, allowing their generations to renew quickly.

Particular resistance to cold, heat, disease, or deprivation should come from Culture, a Talent, or equipment rather than from the Race itself.

Human endurance is average but highly variable. Trained soldiers, riders, sailors, hunters, and travellers can sustain considerable effort for long periods. Their ability to withstand fatigue depends largely on training and willpower.

Humans require regular sleep and possess no special night vision. Their sight, hearing, and other senses are broadly average. Superior ability in perception, tracking, or survival should therefore come from Culture or training.

Adaptability

The defining strength of Humans is their ability to adapt quickly. They live on plains, in mountains and forests, deserts and cold lands, marshes, coasts, and great cities. Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

This ability explains the great variety of human societies. The Hildor may form farming villages, nomadic tribes, trading cities, feudal kingdoms, pastoral societies, or centralized empires.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Professions and character creation

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.

Humans, called Hildor by the Elves, are the Secondborn of the Children of Ilúvatar. They awoke in the East of Middle-earth, in a land called Hildórien, during the First Age. Awareness of mortality strongly shapes human societies. It may foster ambition, the desire for descendants, the wish to leave an enduring work, or the pursuit of glory. It can also create fear of death and the desire to prolong life unnaturally. Sauron often exploited this weakness, most notably among the Númenóreans.

Western traditions distinguish High Men, Common Men, and sometimes Northmen. Most Men live between fifty and eighty years, although life expectancy varies greatly with living conditions and lineage. Some individuals live beyond ninety. Humans reach maturity much faster than Elves and Dwarves, allowing their generations to renew quickly.

Humans require regular sleep and possess no special night vision. Their sight, hearing, and other senses are broadly average. Superior ability in perception, tracking, or survival should therefore come from Culture or training.

The defining strength of Humans is their ability to adapt quickly. They live on plains, in mountains and forests, deserts and cold lands, marshes, coasts, and great cities. Within a few generations, a community may alter its habitat, diet, methods of war, institutions, and language to suit a new environment.

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.

The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.

Family and society

Humans generally have more children than Elves or Dwarves. Family structures, marriage customs, inheritance, and the importance of clans vary greatly from one Culture to another. The Human Race therefore imposes no single family structure.

The same is true of government. Men may live under a clan chief, council, king, prince, autonomous city, or complex administration. Human institutions change rapidly on the scale of Middle-earth’s history.

Crafts, technology, and war

Men can achieve high levels of craftsmanship, engineering, and organization. They practise agriculture, metalworking, construction, navigation, animal husbandry, trade, and fortification. They lack the Khazâd’s special affinity with stone and metal and the ancient lore of the Eldar, but they spread new techniques rapidly.

They have developed nearly every known form of warfare: infantry, cavalry, archers, spearmen, sailors, scouts, and heavy troops. Favoured weapons and armour depend entirely on Culture and available resources.

Languages, religion, and magic

There is no single human language. Westron becomes the principal common tongue of north-western Middle-earth in the later Ages, while Adûnaic, Rohirric, Dunael, Haradaic, Varadja, Logathig, Nahaiduk, and many other languages remain tied to particular peoples.

Human beliefs are equally diverse. Some peoples clearly acknowledge Eru and the Valar; others preserve ancient traditions or have developed local religions. Some societies have also fallen under the influence of Morgoth or Sauron. Humans may practise all the major forms of magic represented by RMU when their Culture and training allow it.

Relations with other peoples

Relations between Men and Elves range from close alliance to mistrust. Relations with the Khazâd are often based on trade, metals, tools, and agricultural goods. Hobbits generally live peacefully alongside neighbouring human communities.

Men also stand at the centre of the wars against the Shadow. Some became the greatest enemies of Morgoth and Sauron, while others entered their service. The Nazgûl themselves were once Men.

Professions and character creation

The Humans — Hildor Race normally forbids no general Profession. Restrictions should instead come from Culture, Age, or the character’s particular background. This Race is available in all four Ages.

After choosing the Human Race, the player selects a human Culture appropriate to the character’s Age and origin. The Dúnedain are handled separately in MERP-UI because of traits inherited from Númenor. The Human Race is intentionally broad: it represents the mortality, diversity, and adaptability shared by the Hildor.
